en: Abhidhānottaratantra, Chapter 28 [Tibetan and Sanskrit, 31] = Lokesh Chandra facsimile edition = 1138 AD palm-leaf manuscript.
[182.2] [Within lacuna:
110–112] Now I shall proclaim the Yoga, the supreme lord of the universal lotus,
the auspicious Great Yoga, the most excellent of all, which bestows great siddhis.
One should meditate through the yoga of the generation stage by means of dissolution;
in the center of a solar mandala, [one sees] Siṃ Oṃ Vaṃ, born from the vajra (= Dhaṃ).
Through the transformation of that, one becomes the supreme Praṇava-Ḍāka.
The Lord of the Universe, possessing all colors, the most excellent among all castes.
Six-faced, twelve-armed, and three-eyed, he is rolling with passion;
he bears the crescent moon, is peaceful, and is adorned with a garland of skulls.
He bears the universal vajra upon his head as a crest tied with matted locks;
his body is arrayed with the six mudrās and adorned with divine ornaments.
Having placed the unfortunate heretics beneath the lotus of the soles of his feet,
he tramples upon the fifteen [deities] by means of the alīḍha stance.
Adorned with the six ornaments and dancing in the half-lotus posture,
they are clothed in Viṣṇu’s hide and decorated with garlands of severed heads.
Absorbed in union with Vajradevī, naked and wearing an excellent girdle,
with loose hair, three eyes, and eight [limbs] pressed together.
Embraced by the vajra-bell, she presses against the positions of the factors of enlightenment;
her two knees are closely joined, and she is eager with the essence of compassion and passion.
Let her be held by the two hands that form the canopy of the Brahma-thread;
let her hold the skull-bowl and the khaṭvāṅga staff, and let her bear the severed head of Maheśvara.
She holds a trident, a sword, and a *ḍamaru* drum, and her hands bear a noose and a goad;
she is fierce in appearance, and her colors are white, blue, green, yellow, smoky, and crimson.
On the left and right sides, two blue-colored Ḍākinīs are joined;
one should place the Vajraḍākinī named Dharmottarā on the left with the syllable *Dhaṃ*.
In the syllable *Siṃ*, there is the Vajraḍākinī named Sāgarottamā;
she is multicolored, with a universal face, three eyes, and a distorted countenance.
She sits in the half-lotus posture, her feet positioned in a dancing stance.
With five faces, ten arms, and three eyes, she is fierce and terrifying;
Bhairava and Kālarātri are situated upon the soles of her lotus feet.
[113] Adorned with ornaments of bone, naked, with disheveled hair, she has a garland of severed heads as her girdle;
her anklets have a jingling sound, and she is decorated with a garland of skulls.
She stands in the center of a lunar mandala, the most supreme among the supreme Ālikālis;
she is adorned with two hands, one brandishing a vajra and the other displaying the tarjanī gesture;
she holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and is further embellished with a hand-drum and a bell.
Holding a noose and a goad in her hands, and another holding a shaven head and a flaying knife.
She who resides in body, speech, and mind as a crown-jewel, the bestower of all accomplishments,
who possesses the means of the meditation on the three wheels and dwells in the midst of the Jñāna-Ḍākinī—
Oṃ is indeed the Jñāna-Ḍāka in the center of the Mind Wheel.
In their hearts are three wives born from the Ḍākas of body, speech, and mind,
through the sequential application of the previously mentioned order by means of the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the sacred seats (pīṭha).
One should cultivate meditative cultivation there, by which [the deities] manifest in succession;
through that cultivation together with the ḍākinī, even the accomplishment is attained for him.
One should recite the mantra while cultivating the state of being of one flavor within the wheel of gnosis.
Oṃ śrīpraṇavaḍāka oṃ āḥ oṃ hūṃ ḍākinījālasamvara oṃ svāhā.
Oṃ hrīḥ, to Padmottamā Mahāvajraḍākinī, dhaṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Oṃ sāṃ, to Sāgarottamā Mahāvajraḍākinī, siṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
By means of the recitation of the secret triple-knowledge, let the Heroine Ḍākinī be recited.
One should join the *praṇava*, one's own name, two *hūṃ*s, and two *phaṭ*s at the end.
The wheel of the three secrets will then flash forth, and one should withdraw it from within the three worlds.
One should meditate upon the secret yoga of the three samayas in the center of the *bhaga*.
The extremely pure Bodhicandra has three wheels; the three women are the principal channels, and there is the triple secret nature.
There is also the triple Dāka and the triple Dākinī, who are supreme in their creation and withdrawal.
Within the *bhagas* of Vajravārāhī, one should meditate upon the cultivation of the triad of the three secrets through the yoga of reality,
with a mind characterized by the secret of the Yoginī.
The yogi should always meditate and likewise recite [mantras] during the four junctions;
he should constantly observe the commitments (samayas), including the "milk" that is the source of the universe.
O Mahābrahmā, for the purpose of taking food, one should consume honey, ghee, and great quantities of meat, consecrated by the three principles (tritattva) with one's own mantra;
doing so without attachment, without hesitation, and free from any sense of avoidance.
One should enjoy those that are faultless and obtained effortlessly;
one should partake of the five strands of sensual pleasure when they are effortless and blameless.
The yogi should drink the soma-liquor, and never any other drink.

One who is joined with internal yoga is presided over by the self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*). The Blessed One is *pīlava* together with the *pīlava*; the *ḍāka* and *ḍākinī* are the secondary *pīlava* (*upapīlava*). Skillful means (*upāya*) is *pīlava*, and wisdom (*prajñā*) is the *yogapīlava*.
The city is Pīlava, and the village is Upapīlava;
through the conjunction of the moon and sun, there is Pīlava and Upapīlava. By means of the moments (kṣaṇa) associated with Pīlava, there are the blameless Upapīlavas.
Endowed with great power, he attains success in this very life;
he may eat the sacrificial animal on the festival day and likewise prepare the *caru* offering.
He should join with *ḍākinīs* and heroes at the gathering (*melāpaka*) held on the festival day.
One should worship the supreme [deity] with offerings of dance and song—
she who is entirely free from conceptual construction and who practices the conduct of the *samaya*.
The twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Signs for the Attainment of the Praṇava-Ḍāka" in the *Abhidhānottarottara*. || 0 ||
